Vs.

case_source: (Arising out of Judgment and decree passed by the District Judge, Comilla).
full_judgment:
A.M. Mahmudur Rahman, J.: In this Rule, the point raised for decision is whether the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) is vested with appellate power to cancel the lease of the disputed land Granted in favour of the petitioner by the Sub-Divisional Officer on 27.1.1975. 

2. The petitioner filed an application on 27.9.1973 praying for settlement of the disputed land measuring .10 decimals appertaining to plot No. 759 contiguous to the homestead of the petitioner. Upon receiving the application, an inquiry was held by the local Tahshilder who submitted report with findings that the land is Government Khas land and fit for cultivation and recommended for settlement of the land. The Circle Officer (Revenue), on receipt of the said report after hearing the petitioner and on perusal of the report and S.A. Khatian, rejected the prayer. The petitioner filed an application for review against the said order before the Circle Officer (Revenue) who sent the application to the Surveyor for physical verification to ascertain whether the land for which settlement was proposed is under Cultivation and possession of the applicant. The surveyor, after verification, submitted his report with a sketch map showing that .10 decimals land out of total land .73 decimals was in Possession of the applicant who has been cultivating the same and it was not required by the public as Rasta. Thereafter, by notice, objection from the public was invited, but as no objection was filed, the Circle Officer (Revenue), on perusal of the report of the Surveyor and other papers, found that the petitioner was the most' deserving candidate for lease of the land and sent a proposal for settlement of the same to the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar, Comilla, who accepted the proposal and granted lease. The petitioner executed a Kabuliyat on payment of Salami in favour of the Government and a Khatian was opened in his name in respect of the said land as tenant and he has been enjoying the land since then under Government. While the petitioner has possessed the land, one Fariduddin, an employee of the Comilla Collectorate, threatened him to dispossess from the said land. He also filed a petition before Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Comilla, in August, 1978, praying for settlement of the suit land in favour, of his brother. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Comilla without any lawful authority treated the same as an appeal and started the settlement case and directed the Circle Officer (Revenue) to submit report on enquiry. On enquiry, the Circle Officer (Revenue) submitted the report against the settlement in favour of the petitioner to which the petitioner filed written objection before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Comilla. But the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Comilla, by an ex-parte order dated 26.6.1979; cancelled the lease granted in favour of petitioner. The petitioner thereafter filed a review petition before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) in vain leading to institution of the Title suit No. 483 of 1979 in the Court of Munsif, Comilla, for declaration that order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) cancelling the lease without any lawful authority on the allegation, inter alia, that the disputed land is the Government Khas land and the same was not "gopath", was under cultivation of his predecissor and thereafter under his cultivation and that was not required for the use of the public as pathway. 

3. The suit was contested by the defendants opposite parties Nos. 1-3 by filing written statement contending that suit land being agricultural land over which there was a drain and a pathway is required for the public use and the same was illegally settled with the plaintiff and as such the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) legally made the order cancelling the lease. 

4. The learned Munsif dismissed the suit holding that the land was not an agricultural land but a pathway and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) was competent to cancell the lease on an application of a third party. 

5. The petitioner appealed before the District Judge against that judgment and decree. The lower appellate Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court giving rise to the present Rule. 

6. Mr. Abul Khair submits that the surveyor having had, reported that the land settled with the plaintiff measuring .10 decimals out of .73 decimals was no longer a gopath and drain and was turned into an agricultural land by cultivating the same by the petitioner and his predecessor who had been in possession of the same and the same not being required by the public as pathway, the lease was granted rightly in favour of the petitioner who satisfied the requirement of Section 76 of State Acquisition & Tenancy Act, 1950. Secondly, placing reliance on Rule 105 of the Government Estate Mannual, he submits that the lower appellate Court erred in holding that upon an application of a third party, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) was competent to cancel the lease as an appellate authority. Rule 105 reads:- 

“১০৫। এই আদেশে জেলা প্রশাসকের উপর প্রদত্ত সকল ক্ষমতা ও দায়িত্ব নিম্নোক্ত কয়টি ক্ষেত্র ছাড়া অতিরিক্ত জেলা প্রশাসক (রাজস্ব) এর প্রতি প্রদত্ত হয়েছে বলে গণ্য করা হবে;-
(ক) প্রদেয় বন্দোবস্ত বাতিল এবং 
(খ) উচ্ছেদ কারণের আদেশ প্রদান”

A mere reading of Rule 105 as quoted above abundantly makes it clear that the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) has not been vested with power to cancel a lease and it is the Deputy Commissioner only who is vested so. Section 147 of the Act is the relevant law on this point which speaks about the forum of appeal. Section 147 reads:- 

“147. Appeals. Subject to any special provisions for appeal made in this part or in any rules made under this Act, an appeal shall tie from every original or appellate order made under any of the provisions of this part by a Revenue Officer as follows, namely:- 

(a) to the collector, when the order is made by a Revenue Officer subordinate to the Collector."

Thus, a close reading of Section 147 indicates that an appeal, whether from original order or from an appellate order, made under any provision of Part V of the Act by a Revenue Officer subordinate to Collector, shall lie to the Collector. Section 148 provides period of limitation for an appeal from an order passed under Section 147. Section 148 reads:- 

"148. Limitation for Appeals. The period of Limitation for an appeal under Section 147 shall run from the date of the order appealed against and shall be as follows, that is to say—

(a) when the appeal lies to the Collector thirty days.
(b) When the appeal lies to the Commissioner of a Division sixty days. 
(b) when the appeal lies to the Government ninety days. 

Thus, from Section 148 it appears that an appeal from an order of the Revenue Officer subordinate to the Collectorate lies to the collector and for such appeal the period of limitation is thirty days. From a careful reading of Section 147 and Rule 105 of the Manual it appears to me that in the instant case, the Deputy Commissioner is the appellate authority and not the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue). Thus, in this case the lower appellate Court committed an crrer of law in its decision in holding that the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) was a competent authority to hear and dispose of the appeal upon an application by a third party inasmuch as no jurisdiction is vested in the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) to hear an appeal by virtue of such application in view of the provision of Section 147 of the Act. 

7. The Assistant Attorney-General argued that the land settled with the petitioner is "dova কৃষির যোগ্য নয়” But from a persusal of the order dated 1.2.1979 it appears that Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) did not discuss the report of the Surveyor and did not discuss the report of the Surveyor and did not refer to the report and also the recommendation made by the Tahshilder earlier as well to the Circle Officer (Revenue) and the application for review filed by the petitioner. The learned Assistant Attorney-General argued that the land being pathway, doba etc. as referred in Rule 22, Register VIII of State Mannual, Chapter III, the Government had settled the same wrongly and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) rightly cancelled the same. He also cited the decision in the case of Jafar Ali-Vs- Khagendra Chandra Dutta and others, 1983 BLD 32. There is no dispute that the nature of the land of that case is quite different from the nature of the land of the instant case. In Jafar Ali's case it was recorded as “সাধারণের জন্য ব্যবহারযোগ্য” and the land was not abandoned by the Hindus as a cremation ground. In view of the finding in the above case the same has no application to the facts of the present case as the Surveyor on local inquiry in the present case found that the pathway is no more in existence on .10 acres of land which is in possession of the plaintiff-petitioner. In this view of the matter, I hold that the judgment of the lower appellate Court cannot also be maintained. As Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) is not vested with the appellate power and the lower appellate Court did not at all consider the material evidence with regard to the nature of the land and the report of the Tahsilder recommending the lease in favour of the petitioner, the lower appellate Court committed an error of law in the decision resulting failure of justice in dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court. Accordingly, the judgments and the decrees of both the Courts below are set aside. 

8. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. No order as to costs. 

End.
